prompt.context: Three friends, Laura, Isabel, and Dom, are creating a t-shirt company called Layup Line Designs, LLC in Nashville, TN. They are annoyed with the lack of 'cool' Nashville-based t-shirts in the market and have decided to take matters into their own hands. They have hired us to think through key considerations in starting this company.
prompt.question: What are the key considerations the three founders should evaluate before launching Layup Line Designs?

clarifying_info.q: Do they want to stay local or expand nationally?
Do they have prior small business experience?
clarifying_info.a: No, they have no experience in small business.

clarifying_info.q: Will they design and print the shirts themselves?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, they plan to both design and screen print, but will source the actual blank t-shirt.

clarifying_info.q: What is the population of Nashville?
clarifying_info.a: The Nashville MSA is 1.8 million; 13 million tourists visit per year.

exhibits.title: P&L with no salary scenario
exhibits.shows: A profit-and-loss table showing variable cost line items per shirt, total variable cost per shirt, average retail price, operating margin per shirt, and annual fixed costs assuming founders take no salary and use a free repurposed basement.

exhibits.title: P&L with salary TBD scenario
exhibits.shows: The same profit-and-loss table as Exhibit 1 but with salary and total fixed costs left as unknowns, to be determined based on the founders' desired compensation.

framework: Profit analysis: revenue per shirt, variable costs per shirt, fixed costs, breakeven volume
Competitive landscape: existing Nashville t-shirt brands, local boutiques, online competitors
Industry trends: custom/local apparel growth, screen printing demand, e-commerce impact
Target customer: Nashville locals vs. tourists, demographics, willingness to pay

questions.prompt: What are the key cost considerations for Layup Line Designs, noting that they will both design and print t-shirts?
questions.guidance: Candidate should structure costs into fixed vs. variable. Fixed costs: founders' salary (initially $0 since they have day jobs), printing equipment, website/marketing. Variable costs: blank t-shirts, ink, screens, transparencies, emulsion. Strong candidates name specific line items for each bucket.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 1, how many t-shirts would they need to sell to break even (annual and per week)? Assume founders take no salary and use a free basement.
questions.guidance: Candidate should state the breakeven formula: Fixed Costs / Unit Contribution Margin. Read inputs from exhibit, set up the equation clearly, then calculate. Weekly volume should assume a 50-week operating year.

math.setup: Breakeven units = Total Fixed Costs / (Revenue per shirt - Variable cost per shirt) = Fixed Costs / Operating Margin per shirt
steps: Weekly breakeven = 500 / 50 weeks = 10 shirts per week
math.answer: 500 shirts per year; 10 shirts per week

questions.prompt: Based on the breakeven calculation, does this seem feasible? What else would you want to consider?
questions.guidance: 10 shirts per week is a low volume and seems achievable as a side business. Candidate should return to the original framework: competitive landscape (are there rival local t-shirt brands?), space constraints in the basement, industry trends, Nashville's large population (1.8M) and tourism (13M/year) providing a sizable addressable market. Should give 2-3 strong, structured reasons.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 2, if Laura, Izzy, and Dom each want to earn a minimum of $50,000/year so they can quit their day jobs, how many t-shirts would they need to sell per year? Per week?
questions.guidance: Candidate must first calculate new total fixed costs by adding three salaries to marketing costs, then apply the breakeven formula. Weekly volume uses a 50-week year.

math.setup: New Fixed Costs = (3 founders x $50,000 salary) + $10,000 marketing. Breakeven = New Fixed Costs / Operating Margin per shirt
steps: Weekly breakeven = 8,000 / 50 weeks = 160 shirts per week
math.answer: 8,000 shirts per year; 160 shirts per week

recommendation: Without salaries, breakeven is easily achievable at 10 shirts per week — the side-business scenario is feasible.
However, if the founders want to quit their day jobs, they need to sell 160 shirts per week (8,000/year), which is dramatically harder to achieve.

This full-time scenario is most likely infeasible in the near term: it would require hiring additional help (raising fixed costs further), renting dedicated space, and capturing a large share of a fragmented local market.
risks: Volume of 160 shirts/week likely requires more staff and rented production space, significantly increasing fixed costs beyond the model assumptions.
Competitive landscape in local/tourist apparel could be crowded; undifferentiated designs risk low repeat purchase.
Tourism is seasonal; 13M annual visitors does not translate uniformly to year-round demand.
No business experience increases execution risk across operations, marketing, and distribution.
next_steps: Validate demand through a small pilot (pop-up or online store) before committing to full-time.
Research direct competitors — local Nashville t-shirt brands and tourist-oriented retailers.
Model sensitivity: recalculate breakeven under realistic scenarios where rent and additional labor are added.
Explore online/e-commerce channel to extend reach beyond local foot traffic.
